subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows increasing levels of organisation?
questions.explain: Cells group into tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together as organ systems to make a whole organism. The order is cell then tissue then organ then organ system.

questions.q: According to the lock and key model, why is each enzyme specific to one substrate?
options: Enzymes are used up in the reaction
The active site has a complementary shape to only one substrate
Enzymes only work at very high temperatures
questions.explain: In the lock and key model the enzyme's active site has a specific shape that is complementary to only one substrate, so each enzyme catalyses one type of reaction. Enzymes are proteins and are not used up.

questions.q: What happens to an enzyme if the temperature rises well above its optimum?
options: The active site changes shape (denatures) and the substrate no longer fits
questions.explain: Above the optimum temperature the enzyme denatures: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits, and the reaction stops. A very high or low pH can also denature enzymes.

questions.q: Proteases break down proteins into which products?
questions.explain: Proteases break proteins down into amino acids. Carbohydrases (e.g. amylase) break carbohydrates into simple sugars, and lipases break lipids into glycerol and fatty acids.

questions.q: What is the role of bile in digestion?
options: It breaks down protein into amino acids
It kills all bacteria in the gut
It neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats to increase surface area
questions.explain: Bile is alkaline so it neutralises the acid from the stomach, and it emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to work. Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

questions.q: A positive result with Benedict's solution (heated) is shown by a colour change from blue to:
questions.explain: Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugars; a positive result changes from blue to brick-red (via green, yellow, orange). Iodine tests for starch (blue-black), Biuret tests protein (purple), and Sudan III/ethanol tests lipids.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to test for the presence of protein?
questions.explain: Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple/lilac when protein is present. Iodine tests for starch, and Benedict's tests for reducing sugars.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood out to the whole body?
questions.explain: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood around the whole body, so it has a thicker muscular wall. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

questions.q: Which feature of arteries suits their function of carrying blood at high pressure?
options: Very thin walls and large lumen
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, so they have thick, elastic, muscular walls. Veins have thinner walls and valves; capillaries have walls one cell thick for exchange.

questions.q: Which blood component transports oxygen and contains haemoglobin?
questions.explain: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin and transports it around the body. They have no nucleus, giving more room for haemoglobin.

questions.q: What is the main role of platelets in the blood?
questions.explain: Platelets are small fragments of cells that help the blood to clot at the site of a wound, preventing blood loss and stopping pathogens entering.

questions.q: In coronary heart disease, what causes the reduced blood flow to the heart muscle?
options: The heart muscle grows too large
There is too much oxygen in the blood
The heart valves become too wide
Layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries
questions.explain: In coronary heart disease, fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood (and so oxygen) flow to the heart muscle. Stents or statins can be used to treat it.

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of using a mechanical (artificial) heart valve compared with a biological one?
options: It removes the need for surgery
The patient must take drugs to prevent blood clots
It only works in young people
questions.explain: Mechanical valves can cause blood clots, so patients must take anti-clotting drugs. Biological valves may wear out sooner. Both require major surgery to fit.

questions.q: Which of these is a risk factor for a non-communicable disease?
options: Smoking, poor diet and lack of exercise
questions.explain: Non-communicable diseases are not spread between people. Lifestyle risk factors such as smoking, poor diet, obesity, alcohol and lack of exercise increase their likelihood, e.g. type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

questions.q: Why can carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke be harmful during pregnancy?
options: It makes the placenta grow larger
It reduces the oxygen the blood can carry to the developing fetus
It increases oxygen supply to the fetus
It has no effect on the fetus
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, reducing the amount of oxygen the blood can carry. During pregnancy this reduces oxygen supply to the fetus, which can lead to low birth weight or premature birth.

questions.q: What is cancer?
options: A communicable disease caused by bacteria
A shortage of white blood cells
The result of uncontrolled cell division forming a tumour
questions.explain: Cancer results from changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division, forming a tumour. Benign tumours stay in one place; malignant tumours can spread (metastasise) to other tissues.

questions.q: Which plant tissue transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots to the leaves?
questions.explain: Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to leaves in the transpiration stream. Phloem transports dissolved sugars (translocation) around the plant in both directions.

questions.q: Transpiration is best described as:
options: The absorption of minerals by roots
The transport of sugars in the phloem
The loss of water vapour from the leaves and stems of a plant
The making of glucose in the leaf
questions.explain: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata in the leaves. This pulls water up the xylem in the transpiration stream. Translocation is the movement of sugars in the phloem.

questions.q: Which condition would INCREASE the rate of transpiration?
options: Increased temperature, wind and light intensity
questions.explain: Higher temperature, more air movement (wind), higher light intensity (stomata open) and lower humidity all increase transpiration rate. High humidity reduces the concentration gradient and slows it down.

questions.q: What is the function of guard cells surrounding a stoma?
options: To transport water up the stem
To open and close the stomata, controlling gas exchange and water loss
questions.explain: Guard cells change shape to open and close the stomata, controlling the exchange of gases (CO2 in, O2 out) and the loss of water vapour. Stomata usually close in the dark or when water is scarce.
